To refuse means to say "no" to something — either to something offered to you, or to something asked of you. But it's not just any "no." When you refuse, you are making a deliberate, conscious choice not to do something or not to accept something. The key ingredient is willingness — refusing is about not wanting to, not about not being able to.

Compare:

  • "I couldn't go to the party." — You were unable to go.
  • "I refused to go to the party." — You were able, but you chose not to.

This distinction is important. Refusing always implies a decision. Something — a request, an offer, an instruction — was placed before you, and you actively chose to push it away.

The verb "refuse" is used in a few different grammatical patterns. Each is common, so it's worth understanding all of them.

Pattern 1: refuse + a thing (noun)

Here, you refuse an object — something offered or given.

She refused the money.
He refused the job offer.
The patient refused the medication.

You were offered something. You said no. That's refusing.

Pattern 2: refuse + to + verb

Here, you refuse to do an action — something asked or expected of you.

She refused to leave.
He refused to apologize.
They refused to follow the order.

This is the most common pattern. Someone wanted you to do something, and you would not.

Pattern 3: refuse + someone + something

Here, you refuse a person by not giving them something they asked for or need.

The bank refused him a loan.
The guard refused them entry.
The school refused the student permission to leave.

Notice the structure: refuse → the person → the thing they wanted. You are withholding something from someone.

Pattern 4: refuse (with nothing after it)

You can also use "refuse" on its own, without saying what specifically was refused, when the context already makes that clear.

I asked him to come, but he refused.
She was offered help many times. She always refused.
What Can Be Refused, and by Whom

Almost any offer, request, instruction, or opportunity can be refused. Common things that are refused include:

  • Requests: "He refused my request for more time."
  • Offers: "She refused the offer of a promotion."
  • Orders: "The soldier refused the order."
  • Invitations: "He refused the dinner invitation."
  • Help: "She refused all help, insisting on doing it herself."
  • Entry or access: "They were refused entry to the building."
  • Food: "The child refused to eat."
  • Permission: "The principal refused permission for the event."
  • Responsibility: "She refused responsibility for what happened."

Mostly, it is people who refuse. But in informal, figurative speech, you can say that a thing "refuses" to work — meaning it simply won't function, almost as if it has a stubborn will of its own.

The car refused to start on a cold morning.
The knot refused to come undone.

This is a figure of speech, treating an object as if it were acting stubbornly. You will encounter this often in everyday English.

"Refuse" is a firm word. It suggests resistance, resolve, and sometimes defiance. When someone refuses, they are holding their ground. The word carries the sense that there was pressure — something expected of them, something pushed toward them — and they did not give in.

This is why "refuse" is often used in dramatic or emotionally significant situations:

She refused to betray her friend, even under pressure.
He refused to give up, despite everything.
The prisoners refused to cooperate with their captors.

It doesn't have to be dramatic, of course — you can casually refuse a biscuit at tea. But the word always retains that sense of a clear, deliberate "no."

Several words are close to "refuse" in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavour.

Decline — This is the more polite, softer version of refuse. When you decline something, you say no courteously, without confrontation. You'd decline an invitation to a wedding; you'd refuse to sign a document under pressure.

"I'm afraid I must decline the invitation." (Polite, formal)
"She refused to sign the document." (Firm, possibly with tension)

Reject — When you reject something, you are not just saying no; you are dismissing it as unworthy, unsuitable, or unacceptable. It carries a harsher judgment.

"The editor rejected the manuscript." (Judged it unfit)
"She refused to read the manuscript." (Simply chose not to)

Deny — To deny means to withhold something from someone, or to say that something is not true. It focuses more on the person being denied than on your act of refusal.

"He was denied bail." (The court withheld bail from him)
"He refused bail." (He chose not to accept it, which can also happen)

Turn down — This is the informal, conversational equivalent of refuse. It means exactly the same thing but sounds more casual and friendly.

"She turned down the job offer." = She refused the job offer.
An Important Nuance: Refusing a Person Directly

When you "refuse someone," you are denying them what they want from you — their request, their attention, their desire.

"He proposed, and she refused him."

This means she said no to his proposal — she declined what he was asking for. The person themselves becomes the object of "refuse," and what they wanted is left implied.
A Few More Examples in Context

To help you see this word in action across different settings:

The suspect refused to answer any questions without a lawyer present.

(Chose not to answer; this was a deliberate decision)

No matter how hungry she was, she refused to beg.

(She held firm; would not do it, even under difficult circumstances)

The committee refused his application for a third time.

(They declined to approve it; withheld acceptance)

He simply refused — no explanation, no apology.

(A complete, final no)

The body sometimes refuses to heal as quickly as we would like.

(Figurative: it doesn't cooperate, as if by stubbornness)

To refuse is to consciously and firmly say no — to something offered, something asked, or something expected. It is about willingness, not ability. It implies a decision, often made in the face of some expectation or pressure. It can be followed by a noun (refuse the offer), by to + verb (refuse to go), or used on its own (she refused). It is stronger than decline, less judgmental than reject, and more formal than turn down. To refuse is to exercise your will and choose not to — clearly, deliberately, and with finality.
